prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed B048 first, but I rest the case on the science, not on that agreement. The work defines a physiological axis: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, and glucose-dependent insulin secretion with satiety effects. It then follows an unusually complete chain into drugs with large randomised outcome trials and global use. The mechanism has been independently confirmed for decades, the clinical benefit extends beyond glycaemia to cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and the interpretation is stable. A prize that honours the physiology (Holst, Drucker) together with the identification of the active peptide (Mojsov) fits the Physiology or Medicine mandate well and gives a compact, defensible three-person group.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is partly disputed, and early peptide and cloning contributors such as Habener are not on the credited list, so a three-name prize may be criticised as incomplete. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide is what put the biology into patients, and leaving her out rewards the discovery side over the development side. The field is also still expanding (neuroprotective and other indications are unproven), so one might argue for waiting. I consider the core discovery and its validation mature enough, but these points should stay on the record.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked B048 first and treated Knudsen's work on long-acting analogues as important but more developmental, with the allocation between basic discovery and drug development not fully settled. He placed B031 (CAR-T) second as a clean and field-changing configuration.
responses.response: I agree that Knudsen sits on the development side and should not displace a basic discoverer within a three-person limit. I would qualify this, though. If we exclude her we should say in the citation that the prize recognises the physiology and the active peptide, not the drug engineering, so that we do not imply the drugs came from the biology alone. On B031 I am less comfortable than he is that Sadelain, June and Rosenberg make a fair trio. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is broader than CAR, and Eshhar's original chimeric receptor is missing from the credited names, so I would keep B031 as an alternative and not a co-equal second part.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked optogenetics (B050) second and noted that the three-person limit forces out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, which he called a real weakness. He also gave weight to enabling technologies in his wider ranking.
responses.response: I share his view that B050 is scientifically very strong, but I disagree that it is ready as a prize configuration. With six credited people and a genuinely split origin (channelrhodopsin discovery against neuronal deployment against Miesenboeck's earlier genetically targeted approach), any three-name choice would be contested and could be read as an editorial judgement on who matters. It is also a research tool whose medical payoff, such as vision restoration, is still early. That is why I keep it as an alternative and do not combine it with B048 as a second part.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked B048 first and also placed cGAS-STING (B044) fourth, with Chen and Barber as a supportable two-person core. He accepted that therapeutic translation of STING is still maturing.
responses.response: I accept that the Chen and Barber pairing is mechanistically clear. My reservation is maturity. No approved STING-targeted therapy exists, the question of whether to include Ishikawa, Wu and Sun is open, and this is therefore a candidate for a later year, not this one. I would not give it a part in a two-achievement prize now.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B001) second as a clean Feldmann and Maini pairing with a clear mechanism-to-therapy logic, and ranked B048 first on the basis that the basic discoveries are the more prize-appropriate core over Knudsen's industrial translation.
responses.response: I agree with her reasoning on B048, which is the same logic I use for excluding Knudsen. On B001 I recognise the pairing is clean and the impact is large, but I would ask whether it is a clinical-translation prize whose upstream TNF biology and antibody engineering is credited to others. She raises a fair point that the field has waited long, so I would keep B001 in view for a later discussion without making it one of my two alternatives.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked B048 first but flagged that priority over the active GLP-1 peptide is unresolved and that Habener and other early contributors are not on the credited list. He picked B050 second and B031 third.
responses.response: This is the most serious attribution objection to my own configuration, and I do not think the supplied material resolves it. My position is that Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a distinct and necessary step, and that a prize which names Holst, Drucker and Mojsov is defensible, but we must treat the possibility of omitting Habener-group contributions as a real cost. I share his ordering of B050 and B031 behind B048 only as alternatives, since both carry attribution problems that are at least as severe as the one he raises for B048.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or an alternative contributor (for example Knudsen on the development side) is the right third name, given priority disputes I cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether the committee should treat a physiology-led prize as sufficient or add a second, distinct part, and whether B031 or B050 could be configured fairly with the credited names.
Whether the maturity of the incretin field is sufficient given still-developing evidence on long-term safety and non-metabolic indications.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent between my profile and any shortlisted ballot. My Rockefeller postdoc with Paul Greengard and my roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy) do not involve any shortlisted candidate. The remaining shortlisted candidates, including optogenetics, are outside my own research.
